heading: From Harappa to a partitioned province
body: Punjab's history begins earlier than almost anywhere else in South Asia: Harappa, on the banks of the now-shifted Ravi river, was one of the two great cities of the Indus Valley Civilisation, inhabited from around 2600 to 1900 BCE and rediscovered by archaeologists — after 19th-century railway builders had literally quarried its ancient bricks for ballast — in excavations beginning in 1921. Its grid-planned streets, citadel and standardised weights place Punjab at the very start of subcontinental urban history, roughly contemporary with Mesopotamia and Egypt's early dynasties.

Millennia later, the region became the base of the last great pre-colonial Indian empire. Guru Nanak founded Sikhism in Punjab in the late 15th century, and his successors built it into an organised faith and military community, the Khalsa. Out of the 18th-century Sikh misls (confederacies), Ranjit Singh unified Punjab under a single Sikh Empire in 1799, ruling from Lahore over a religiously mixed administration that stretched from the Khyber Pass to the Sutlej until his death in 1839. Internal succession struggles and two Anglo-Sikh wars ended in British annexation of Punjab in 1849.

Partition in 1947 cut directly through Punjab rather than around it: the province was split along religious lines between India and the new Pakistan, uprooting millions of Hindus, Muslims and Sikhs in one of history's largest and most violent mass migrations, and leaving Lahore — the seat of Ranjit Singh's empire — on the Pakistani side of a new border. The places mapped here trace that long line from Harappa's Bronze Age streets through the Sikh Empire's forts and gurdwaras to the towns reshaped by 1947.

sources.title: The Real History of Punjab Before 1947: From Harappa to Partition — Pindblock
